rows.title: Fault (geology)
rows.text: Since faults do not usually consist of a single, clean fracture, geologists use the term fault zone when referring to the zone of complex deformation associated with the fault plane.

rows.title: Fault (geology)
rows.text: Based on direction of slip, faults can be categorized as:

rows.title: Fault (geology)
rows.text: Dip-slip faults can be either "normal" ("extensional") or "reverse".

rows.title: Fault (geology)
rows.text: A reverse fault is the opposite of a normal fault—the hanging wall moves up relative to the footwall. Reverse faults indicate compressive shortening of the crust. The dip of a reverse fault is relatively steep, greater than 45°.

rows.title: Fault (geology)
rows.text: A thrust fault has the same sense of motion as a reverse fault, but with the dip of the fault plane at less than 45Â°.[9][10] Thrust faults typically form ramps, flats and fault-bend (hanging wall and foot wall) folds.

rows.title: Fault (geology)
rows.text: Flat segments of thrust fault planes are known as flats, and inclined sections of the thrust are known as ramps. Typically, thrust faults move within formations by forming flats and climb up sections with ramps.

rows.title: Fault (geology)
rows.text: Fault-bend folds are formed by movement of the hanging wall over a non-planar fault surface and are found associated with both extensional and thrust faults.

rows.title: Fault (geology)
rows.text: Faults may be reactivated at a later time with the movement in the opposite direction to the original movement (fault inversion). A normal fault may therefore become a reverse fault and vice versa.
